items.q: Teen hit the side of his head, was fine for an hour, now drowsy. What is the bright collection against the skull?
items.why: Lens-shaped (biconvex) bright blood pressed against the skull: an epidural hematoma. It can't cross the suture lines because the dura is stuck there. Usually arterial (middle meningeal artery under a temporal bone fracture). Treatment: emergency craniotomy and evacuation.

items.q: Older adult on blood thinners fell a few days ago, now confused. What's the crescent along the brain surface?
items.why: A crescent that follows the curve of the brain and can cross sutures: a subdural hematoma from torn bridging veins. Fresh blood is bright, older blood turns grey then dark. Big or symptomatic ones are drained (burr holes or craniotomy).

items.q: Compare both sides of the brain carefully. What do you see?
items.why: Thin crescents on both sides between the skull and brain: bilateral subdural hematomas. Because both sides push equally, there may be little midline shift, which makes them easy to miss. Always compare the two sides.

cr.a: Dr. George Jallo, pediatric neurosurgeon at Johns Hopkins

items.q: Worst headache of her life, hit in seconds. What does the CT show?
items.why: Bright blood filling the CSF spaces around the base of the brain (basal cisterns) and in the fissures: subarachnoid hemorrhage, most often from a ruptured aneurysm. Next step: CT angiogram to find it, then coiling or clipping.

items.q: Man with long-standing high blood pressure, sudden one-sided weakness. What is the bright area deep in the brain?
items.why: A rounded bright clot inside the brain tissue near the basal ganglia: hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage. Chronic high pressure weakens small penetrating arteries (lenticulostriates). Fresh blood is bright on CT. Management: lower BP, reverse blood thinners, surgery for some large bleeds.

items.q: Large bright area in one hemisphere. What is it, and where else has it spread?
opts: Intracerebral hemorrhage spreading into the ventricles
items.why: A big intracerebral hemorrhage that has broken into the ventricular system (blood layering in the ventricles). Blood in the ventricles can block CSF flow and cause hydrocephalus, which may need an external ventricular drain.

items.q: Stroke symptoms started 2 days ago. What is the dark area in one hemisphere?
items.why: Dead, swollen brain holds extra water, so it looks darker (hypodense) on CT, in the shape of an arterial territory (here the middle cerebral artery). In the first hours a CT is often still normal: it's done mainly to exclude bleeding before clot-busting treatment.

items.q: Big dark areas on one side, including the back of the brain. Which arterial territories?
items.why: Dark tissue over the lateral hemisphere (middle cerebral artery) AND the occipital lobe (posterior cerebral artery). Some people's PCA branches off the internal carotid (fetal PCA), so one carotid blockage can hit both.

items.q: Diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI) of a stroke patient. What does the bright spot mean?
opts: Acute infarct: water can't move freely
items.why: In an acute infarct, cells swell (cytotoxic edema) and water can't diffuse, so DWI lights up within minutes, long before CT changes. DWI is the most sensitive test for an early stroke.

items.q: Headache and vomiting, worse in the morning. What's abnormal?
items.why: Ballooned ventricles with squashed sulci: hydrocephalus (too much CSF under pressure). Atrophy also makes big ventricles, but then the sulci are big too. Treatment is draining CSF: a shunt or endoscopic third ventriculostomy.

items.q: T1 MRI with contrast. A ring-enhancing mass with a dark centre and swelling around it. Most likely?
items.why: Thick irregular ring of enhancement around a dead (necrotic) centre inside the brain: classic glioblastoma, the most common malignant primary brain tumour in adults. Main mimic: abscess (check DWI). Treatment: maximal safe surgical resection, then radiotherapy plus an alkylating chemotherapy drug (temozolomide class).

items.q: Contrast MRI: smooth, brightly enhancing mass attached to the covering of the brain, pushing on it from outside. Most likely?
items.why: An extra-axial (outside the brain) mass with a broad base on the dura and even, bright enhancement: meningioma, usually benign, from arachnoid cap cells. Small ones are watched; growing or symptomatic ones are removed surgically or treated with radiosurgery.

cr.t: Intracranial bleed with significant midline shift.png

items.q: What is the most dangerous finding on this scan?
opts: Midline shift from a large mass
items.why: A large lesion pushing the midline structures to the other side: midline shift. It means pressure inside the skull is high and the brain is close to herniating, so this needs urgent treatment of the cause (often neurosurgery).

items.q: Large subdural hematoma on one side. What is happening to the brain?
opts: It is herniating: pushed across the midline under the falx
An epidural bleed on the other side
items.why: The clot pushes the hemisphere under the falx cerebri (subfalcine herniation) and squashes the ventricle. Further pressure can force the temporal lobe over the tentorium (uncal herniation), compressing CN III and the brainstem.

items.q: Normal head CT. Swipe through it top to bottom. Why is the skull white, the brain grey and the ventricles dark?
opts: CT shade = density: bone densest, CSF like water, air black
Bone has the most blood flow
items.why: CT measures how much each tissue blocks X-rays (Hounsfield units). Bone ≈ +1000 (white), fresh blood ≈ +60 (bright), brain ≈ +30–40 (grey), CSF/water ≈ 0 (dark grey), fat negative, air ≈ −1000 (black).

cr.t: CT of a normal brain, axial 1–38

items.q: Scroll to a slice that shows the lateral ventricles (dark C or butterfly shapes in the middle), then tap “This one”.
items.why: The lateral ventricles sit in the middle of each hemisphere. Their bodies and frontal horns look like a dark butterfly on slices around the level of the top of the thalamus.

cr.t: CT of a normal brain, axial 1–38

items.q: Scroll to a slice through the eyeballs (orbits).
items.why: The globes appear as round grey circles at the front, with the bright lens and the optic nerves running back toward the middle. That level also shows the temporal lobes and the pons.

cr.t: CT of a normal brain, axial 1–38

items.q: Scroll down to a slice that shows the cerebellum at the back of the head.
items.why: Low slices show the posterior fossa: cerebellum at the back, brainstem in front of it with the 4th ventricle between. Bone around the skull base causes streaky artifacts here, one reason MRI is better for the posterior fossa.

cr.t: CT of a normal brain, axial 1–38

items.q: Look at a slice near the top. On CT, which is slightly brighter?
items.why: Grey matter is a bit denser than white matter (white matter has fatty myelin), so the cortex looks slightly brighter on CT. Losing that grey-white difference is an early sign of an ischemic stroke.

items.q: Older adult with a shuffling walk, leaking urine and memory trouble. Scroll through. What is the key finding?
opts: Ventricles much larger than the sulci: hydrocephalus
items.why: The ventricles are ballooned out of proportion to the sulci: hydrocephalus. With 'wet, wobbly and wacky' (incontinence, gait trouble, confusion) in an older person, think normal pressure hydrocephalus. Treatment: a ventriculoperitoneal shunt. The bright dot inside the right lateral ventricle, which tracks up to a hole in the skull on the top slices, looks like a shunt catheter.

items.q: MRI of someone whose glioblastoma was operated on years earlier. Scroll up. The large dark fluid-filled hole in the left frontal lobe is most likely…
items.why: After a tumour is removed, the space fills with CSF and looks dark like fluid: the resection cavity. Glioblastoma usually comes back at the edges of the cavity (this scan was taken when it regrew, 5 years after surgery), so follow-up MRIs watch the rim for new enhancement. Remember scan view: the patient's left is on your right.

items.q: Normal T1 MRI. Swipe through it. On T1, which is brighter?
items.why: On T1, fat is bright, so myelin-rich white matter is brighter than grey matter and CSF is dark. On T2 it flips: CSF is bright. Quick trick: if the ventricles are dark, it's probably T1.
